## One Computer, Seven Machines {.smaller}

A program runs on one computer. But the machine you *imagine* while you read it
is a different machine at every layer — and that imagined machine is the one you
actually program.

> **Notional machine** (du Boulay, 1986): the computer you imagine while you read
> a program — what things exist, what they do, and what happens next.

::: {.fragment}
It is not in the hardware. It is taught. And no error message will ever tell you
that yours is wrong.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the whole lecture in one sentence: one computer, seven machines.

Say the definition out loud and give them a moment. The key move is that the
notional machine is a property of *the person*, not of the machine — which is
why two people can read the same line of code and disagree about what it does,
and why "it should work" is never an argument.

The fragment is the reason this lecture is in a course that is not about
programming: nobody will ever hand you a diagnostic that says "your mental model
is broken". You get a wrong answer and no explanation, or an error message about
a symptom rather than a cause.
:::

## The Ladder {.smaller}

![](figs/fig-ladder.svg){height=470px}

Each rung is implemented by the rung below it. Each rung up buys you expression
and costs you visibility.

::: {.notes}
Point at the bottom and the top. The bottom rung is last Wednesday's lecture —
gates, which is the lowest thing that computes and which has no notion of a step
at all. The top is a search engine, which has no notion of a step either. The
middle is where steps live, and that is not a coincidence.

The two arrows are the two halves of the story: going up you can say more and
see less. Going down, everything you can say is *implemented* by something
simpler — which is the only reason the tower stands up.

Tell them the shape of the lecture: one job, climbed one rung at a time, and at
each rung we look at the same two questions — what is a step, and where does the
state live?
:::

# Part 0 — The Machine That Is Actually There

![](figs/fig-ladder-1.svg){height=300px}

Rungs 1 and 2: the machine you can see all of.

## The Computer Knows Three Moves {.smaller}

![](figs/fig-fetch.svg){height=380px}

One instruction can do one of three things:

- arithmetic on two numbers,
- load or store a word of memory,
- change which instruction runs next.

Then repeat, forever.

::: {.notes}
This is the only machine that is genuinely there. Everything above it is
something we agree to pretend, and this slide is the baseline you measure the
pretending against.

The three moves are worth naming precisely because they are so few: no addition
of a *list*, no "if this is even", no "call this function". Those are all
compositions of the three.

The program counter is the part people forget. A computer is not just a
calculator that does the next thing — it holds the *address* of the next thing,
and the ability to overwrite that address is what makes loops and choices
possible.
:::

## One Job, All the Way Up {.smaller}

The job: **sum the squares of the even numbers** in a list. For `[1 2 3 4]` the
answer is **20**.

| what the job needs | so every machine must provide |
|---|---|
| somewhere to keep a running total | storage that survives a step |
| `x * x`, and `+` | arithmetic |
| "only the even ones" | a way to choose |
| "every element of the list" | a way to repeat |

::: {.fragment}
> Every rung has to be able to do this one job. That is what makes the rungs
> comparable — and what makes their differences interesting.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not skip this slide; it is what stops the lecture from being a tour.

Pick a job with all four ingredients, because a job with only arithmetic would
not need most of what the upper rungs provide. Every language in the deck has to
express a choice and a repetition, and the *way* it does that is the layer's
personality.

Ask the room for the answer for [1 2 3 4] before saying it: evens 2 and 4,
squares 4 and 16, total 20. Small enough to check by hand all lecture, which is
the point — every trace today ends at 20, and they can check every one.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a *model* machine, not x86: one instruction per address, word-addressed,
data starting at 100 so program and data never collide. Say so, and say why —
the point is the shape of the trace, not the encoding. On a real x86 one
instruction is a few bytes, and `add %rbx,%rax` is `48 01 d8`.

Click through it slowly, and after every frame ask the room "what changed?".
The lit row is the instruction being executed, the amber register is what just
changed, the blue cell is what was just read, the green cell is what was just
written.

Do not skip passes. The point of stepping all twenty-nine instructions is that
the audience watches the jump at address 09 take them back to address 03, four
times over, and sees the loop for what it is: two jumps and a counter. The
header keeps count — "pass 2 of 4, step 9 of 29" — so nobody loses their place.

Two frames carry the whole lecture. `AND R4, R3, 1` turns "is it even" into a
single bit. `JUMPNZ R4, 8` turns "if it is odd, skip" into a jump. Choice is
arithmetic plus a jump.

Look at what is in the state: registers, memory, and the program counter.
Nothing else exists. There is nowhere else for anything to be.
:::

some only add legibility. This one only adds legibility — and it is still worth
having, because address 03 tells you nothing and `again:` tells you everything.
:::

# Part I — Rung 3: The Stack

![](figs/fig-ladder-3.svg){height=300px}

Rung 3: the first thing in the machine that the hardware has never heard of.

## Variables Are Boxes in a Frame {.smaller}

::: {.steps style="height:560px"}

![](figs/fig-c-01.svg)

![](figs/fig-c-02.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-03.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-04.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-05.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-06.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-07.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-08.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-09.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-10.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-11.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-12.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-c-13.svg){.fragment}

:::

::: {.notes}
Now the state has grown a column: the frame. `total` is not a register and not a
name the hardware knows — it is four bytes at an address the compiler picked,
0x7ffd10, and `i` is the four bytes after it.

Click through and watch `total` change at 0x7ffd10. That address is the point:
the frame is a *place*, and the values in it are just memory.

The array is at 0xa0 and the frame is at 0x7ffd10, and the frame holds a pointer
to the array — that is a lot of structure C invented and the chip knows nothing
about.

The trace is longer than rung 1's, which is honest: a higher-level language has
more state to track, not less. That is the visibility you are paying.
:::

## The Frame Is Not in the Chip {.smaller}

The hardware has registers and memory. It has no idea what a function call is.

- A **frame** is a range of stack memory that the compiler decided to use for one
  call's locals.
- **Scope** is a rule about which frame a name resolves to — it exists in the
  compiler, not in the machine.
- A **return** is "put the result in a register, restore the stack pointer, jump".

::: {.fragment}
> Everything you can *see* in the trace is real memory. Everything that makes it
> a *frame* is a convention someone maintains.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the first rung where the notional machine contains something the hardware
has never heard of, so slow down here — the same move happens at every rung above.

A frame is not a mysterious thing: it is a contiguous chunk of the stack, and
the compiler emits instructions that keep a register (the frame pointer, or the
stack pointer) pointing at it. If you delete those instructions, the frame stops
existing. It is real in the sense that the bytes are real, and invented in the
sense that the *grouping* is a decision.

The practical payoff: this is why a stack overflow is a real thing that can
happen, and why recursion has a cost per call, and why a local variable has an
address. All three are consequences of rung 3's invention.
:::

# Part II — Rung 4: Rewriting the Text

![](figs/fig-ladder-4.svg){height=300px}

Rung 4: the state stops being memory and becomes the program itself.

## A Step Can Be a Rewrite {.smaller}

```scheme
(define (sqs xs)
  (cond ((null? xs) 0)
        ((even? (car xs)) (+ (* (car xs) (car xs)) (sqs (cdr xs))))
        (else (sqs (cdr xs)))))
```

The rule: to evaluate a call, **substitute the arguments into the body**, then
keep going.

::: {.formula}
(+ (* 2 2) (* 3 3))  →  (+ 4 9)  →  13
:::

The syntax *is* the tree — you can see which subtree is being replaced.

::: {.notes}
This is the rung where the notional machine changes *kind*, so do not rush it.

Read the expression out loud: "the sum of two squared and three squared". Then
show that the parentheses already say that — the shape of the text is the shape
of the computation. In `2*2 + 3*3` you have to know a precedence table to recover
the tree; in `(+ (* 2 2) (* 3 3))` the tree is the text.

The substitution rule, in one sentence: replace a call by its body with the
arguments substituted. That is the whole evaluator. Everything else is which
subexpression you choose to rewrite next.

If they have never seen prefix notation: `(+ 1 2)` means "apply + to 1 and 2".
That is 90 seconds and it is the only new syntax in the lecture.
:::

## The State Is the Program {.smaller}

::: {.steps style="height:600px"}

![](figs/fig-s-01.svg)

![](figs/fig-s-02.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-s-03.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-s-04.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-s-05.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-s-06.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-s-07.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-s-08.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-s-09.svg){.fragment}

:::

::: {.notes}
Look at what the state is now: the program text. There are no registers and no
memory cells on this panel, because there is nothing to keep — the expression
*is* the thing that changes.

Each frame highlights the subexpression that is about to be rewritten, then
shows what it becomes. That is the whole evaluator: pick a subexpression,
replace it by its value, repeat. Leftmost-innermost, so the innermost expression
on the left goes first.

Read the highlights down the sequence: `(sqs ...)` unfolds, then `(* 2 2)`
becomes 4, then the next `(sqs ...)` unfolds. The sum is built by the expression
growing and then collapsing — nothing is ever stored.

A literal trace would also show the `cond` clauses being tested one at a time.
We skip those because they are four uninteresting rewrites per element; say so,
so nobody thinks the panel is hiding a trick.
:::

## This Is Not What the Computer Does {.smaller}

A real Scheme does not rewrite text. It keeps environments and a stack of
pending operations, and it compiles to the same three machine moves as everything
else.

::: {.fragment}
> The substitution trace is a **model**. And a model of the machine you should
> imagine while reading a program is exactly what a notional machine is.
:::

::: {.notes}
The most intellectually honest slide in the deck, and the one worth a minute.

There is a real tension: the trace on the previous slide is *not* what a Scheme
implementation does. It does not build new program texts; it keeps an
environment and a continuation. So the trace is a fiction.

It is a *useful* fiction, and it is the fiction SICP teaches, because it predicts
every answer correctly and it is small enough to hold in your head. And that is
the definition we started with: the machine you imagine, not the machine that is
there.

Say the general lesson: every rung in this ladder is a fiction that the rung
below makes true. Rung 4's fiction is enforced by an interpreter at rung 1.
:::

# Part III — Rung 5: Values That Don't Change

![](figs/fig-ladder-5.svg){height=300px}

Rung 5: the same machine as rung 4, with a different idea about data.

## Stop Overwriting, Start Transforming {.smaller}

::: {.steps style="height:450px"}

![](figs/fig-k-01.svg)

![](figs/fig-k-02.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-k-03.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-k-04.svg){.fragment}

:::

::: {.notes}
Clojure is a Scheme — same parentheses, same rewriting machine — so this rung is
deliberately the *same* machine with a different idea about data.

The code is three words: keep, square, add. Read the pipeline right to left,
which is how it runs: filter the evens, map the square, reduce with +. The panel
fills one stage at a time, and each stage builds a new value rather than
changing an old one.

Point out what is *absent*: no `total`, no `i`, no loop, and no line that
changes anything. There is no variable being updated anywhere in this program.

The cost: you can no longer predict what a line costs from the text alone.
`filter` might be eager or lazy; `reduce` might be parallel. You traded
visibility for expression, again.
:::

## The Same Machine, Less Typing {.smaller}

| | rung 4 (Scheme) | rung 5 (Clojure) |
|---|---|---|
| the machine | rewrite the text | rewrite the text |
| who does the recursion | you write it | `filter` / `map` / `reduce` |
| lines in the trace | 10 | 4 |
| anything overwritten | no | no |

::: {.fragment}
> Same machine, one level of thinking moved into the library. That is what a
> library *is*: someone else's notional machine, ready to use.
:::

::: {.notes}
Be precise: rung 5 is not a new kind of machine. The rewriting rule is identical.
What changed is where the recursion lives — you moved it into three functions
that somebody else wrote, and you no longer see it.

That is worth generalising, because it is the main thing that happens as you go
up the ladder: you stop writing the mechanism and start naming it. `filter` is a
loop you did not write.

The cost column is the honest one: you can no longer predict what a line costs
from the text alone. `filter` might be eager or lazy; `reduce` might be
parallel. You traded visibility for expression, again.
:::

# Part IV — Rung 6: The Machine With No Steps

![](figs/fig-ladder-6.svg){height=300px}

Rung 6: the top of the ladder, and the end of steps.

## Declare, Don't Compute {.smaller}

```clojure
(run* [x] (membero x [1 2 3 4]) (pred x even?))
;=> (2 4)
```

```clojure
(run* [x] (membero x [1 2 3 4]) (pred x even?) (pred x #(> % 3)))
;=> (4)
```

There is no loop. You state what must be true of the answer, and the machine
finds values that make it true.

::: {.fragment}
> Adding a condition is not editing a program. It is adding a **fact**.
:::

::: {.notes}
`run*` means "find every answer"; `x` is the variable we are asking about; each
line inside is a *goal* that must hold. Read the second query as a sentence:
"find an x that is in the list, is even, and is greater than 3".

In rung 3 you would have edited the `if` to add that third condition. Here you
appended a goal and the same machine answered a different question. That is the
difference between *how* and *what*, and it is the whole point of the rung.

Both answers are verified — these are real core.logic runs, not a sketch.
:::

## One Relation, Four Questions {.smaller}

::: {.steps style="height:520px"}

![](figs/fig-q-01.svg)

![](figs/fig-q-02.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-q-03.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-q-04.svg){.fragment}

:::

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff of the rung, so give it time. Write the relation on the board
as a sentence: "l then s is o". Nothing about direction, nothing about which one
you know.

Then click through the four questions. The first is the one you would write by
hand at rung 3. The second and third are the ones a loop *cannot* answer — to
solve for the front of the list with a loop you would write a different
function. The fourth returns every way to split the list, and there are five.

Every answer on these panels came from a real run; the parentheses are what
core.logic printed.
:::

## The Trace Is a Tree {.smaller}

::: {.steps style="height:620px"}

![](figs/fig-l-01.svg)

![](figs/fig-l-02.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-03.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-04.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-05.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-06.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-07.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-08.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-09.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-10.svg){.fragment}

![](figs/fig-l-11.svg){.fragment}

:::

::: {.notes}
Look at the shape. Every rung below produced a *line* — a sequence of steps.
This rung produces a tree, because the machine has to try something, fail, and
come back.

Step through it: each level tries clause 1 (the left list is empty, so we have
an answer) and then clause 2 (the left list has a head, so recurse on the tail).
The staircase is the recursion; the answers are the leaves.

The last frame is the payoff: the final clause 2 fails because there is no head
left to take. That failure is not an error — it is how the search knows to stop.

The numbers are the search order, and the answers come out in that order. That
is a general fact about depth-first search, and it is why the printed order of
`(run* ...)` is informative.

This figure is drawn from the engine's own tree, and the engine is checked
against a real core.logic run, so the picture cannot drift from the truth.
:::

## What "Running" Means Here {.smaller}

There is no next instruction. The state is a **substitution** (what we have
learned so far) plus a **frontier** (what is left to try).

- **unify** — make two terms equal by binding variables
- **backtrack** — when a goal fails, undo the last choice and try the next

::: {.fragment}
The engine underneath is a search. That is the same machine as last week's SAT
solver — and it is what is running inside a package manager deciding whether your
dependencies can be installed.
:::

::: {.notes}
The three words that carry the whole rung: substitution, unification, backtracking.

Contrast the state with the rungs below. Rung 1's state was registers and memory.
Rung 3's state was a stack of frames. Rung 4's state was the program text. Now
the state is *what we know* plus *what we have not tried yet* — and there is no
"where" at all.

Close the loop with last week: the boolean deck ended on SAT, a search for an
assignment that makes a formula true. This rung is that search, wearing
parentheses. Nobody wrote a loop; somebody wrote a search engine and a
description of the answer.
:::

# Part V — Above and Below

![](figs/fig-ladder.svg){height=300px}

Where this leaves you, and what is above.

## Every Abstraction Leaks {.smaller}

| what you see | what is really happening |
|---|---|
| `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004` | rung 1: floats are not decimals |
| a stack overflow | rung 3: the frame stack is finite and real |
| "this one line is slow" | rung 1: it is still a loop, whatever it is called |
| a lazy sequence realising at a strange moment | rung 5: the pipeline is not free |

::: {.fragment}
> A leak is the layer below showing through. When something makes no sense,
> ask which rung you are actually standing on.
:::

::: {.notes}
You already met the first one in week 3, in the numbers lecture: 0.1 and 0.2 are
not representable in binary floating point, so their sum is not 0.3. That is not
a bug in the language; it is rung 1 showing through rung 4.

The practical advice is the useful part: when a program surprises you, the
question to ask is not "why is the computer wrong" but "which layer am I
actually standing on, and what does that layer promise". Most confusing bugs are
a layer boundary, not a mistake.

This is also why the notional machine matters: a leak is what it feels like when
your imagined machine and the real one disagree.
:::

## You Already Use Three Declarative Machines {.smaller}

| machine | you say | it works out |
|---|---|---|
| **SQL** | which rows you want | how to find them |
| **a spreadsheet** | a formula per cell | what order to recompute |
| **an LLM prompt** | what you want, in English | the steps (sometimes) |

None of these asks you for a loop. All three are the same move as rung 6: state
the answer, let the machine search.

::: {.notes}
This is where the lecture stops being about programming languages and becomes
about their lives. Most students have written a spreadsheet formula and many have
prompted a model; almost none have written SQL, so explain it in one line.

The spreadsheet is the best example to dwell on, because they have all felt the
dependency graph: change one cell and the whole sheet recomputes in an order you
never specified. That is a declarative machine with a search underneath it.

The LLM is the honest top of the ladder, and the reason November's project looks
the way it does: you describe the result and something else decides the steps.
Say that we will come back to it, and that it is the least reliable machine on
the list — for exactly the reason that it is the most hidden.
:::

## The Language You Will Actually Write {.smaller}

We are not going to write six languages. You will write one: **JavaScript**, or
**TypeScript**.

It is a synthesis of the rungs you just climbed:

- frames and locals — rung 3
- objects on a heap, garbage collected — rung 4
- `map`, `filter`, `reduce` on arrays — rung 5
- and an event loop, which is a search you never see

::: {.fragment}
> The point of the ladder was never to learn six languages. It was to be able to
> see the parts of the one you use.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff for a course that is not about programming: they will write
one language, and now they can look at it and see which rung each feature came
from.

Do it concretely on the slide: a `for` loop is rung 3. An object you pass around
and mutate is rung 4, and the aliasing surprises they will hit in the lab are
rung 4 leaks. `xs.filter(...).map(...)` is rung 5 and they will meet it in the
first week of real code. The event loop is the interesting one — it is a frontier
of pending work, which is rung 6's shape, and it is why `await` exists.

Do not teach any of it. Just point.
:::

## The Ladder Is a Loop {.smaller}

The bottom rung is last Wednesday: gates, which compute with no notion of a step.

The top rung is last Wednesday too: a search for an assignment, which is the SAT
problem the boolean lecture ended on.

::: {.fragment}
> Seven machines, one computer. And the course you are in is the ladder: bits,
> then files, then gates, then instructions, then languages — and now you know
> what is above languages.
:::

::: {.notes}
The structural joke worth landing: we started at gates and ended at a search, and
last week's lecture also started at gates and ended at a search. The middle is
what we climbed today.

Point at the whole course on this slide. Weeks 2 and 3 were rung 1 seen as data:
bytes, numbers, text, files. Week 8 was rung 0. Today was rungs 1 to 6. The
vibe-coding project is the rung above rung 6.

The one sentence to leave in the room: the tower stands because every layer is
implemented by the one below it — and it is worth knowing which floor you are on.
:::

## Five Things to Remember {.smaller}

1. A program is one thing. The machine you *imagine* while reading it is another,
   and it changes with the layer.
2. Each layer is implemented by the layer below it. That is the only reason the
   tower stands.
3. Going up buys expression and costs visibility. Every rung pays that price.
4. The state moves: memory → the program text → a search frontier.
5. The trace changes shape: a line, then a tree.

::: {.notes}
If they remember one thing, make it number 3, because it is the one that pays off
outside this course: any time a tool makes something easier, ask what it just
made invisible.

Number 4 is the summary of the six traces they just watched, and it is worth
saying that they have now seen the same job evaluated six different ways — and
that every one of them was correct.

For the lab and Wednesday: we will write JavaScript, and the question to keep
asking is "which machine am I imagining right now".
:::
